'''Ludwig Schlesinger''' (Hungarian: Schlesinger Lajos, Slovak: Ľudovít Schlesinger), (1 November 1864 &ndash; 15 December 1933) was a [[Germans|German]] [[mathematician]] known for the research in the field of [[linear differential equation]]s.<ref>Gottwald, Ilgauds, Schlote ''Lexikon bedeutender Mathematiker'', Bibliographisches Institut, Leipzig 1990</ref>

==Biography==
Schlesinger attended the high school in [[Pressburg]] and later studied physics and mathematics in [[Heidelberg]] and [[Berlin]]. In 1887 he received his PhD (Über lineare homogene Differentialgleichungen vierter Ordnung, zwischen deren Integralen homogene Relationen höheren als ersten Grades bestehen.) His thesis advisors were [[Lazarus Immanuel Fuchs]] and [[Leopold Kronecker]]. In 1889 he became an associate professor at Berlin; in 1897 an invited professor in [[Bonn]] and in the same year, a full professor at the [[University of Kolozsvár]], [[Hungary]] (now Cluj, Romania). From 1911 he was professor at the [[University of Giessen]], where he taught until 1930. His daughter [[Hildegard Lewy]] (1903–1969), became an Assyriologist and academic. In 1933 he was forced to retire by the [[Nazis]]. He died shortly afterwards.<ref>{{cite book|chapter-url=https://www.biographien.ac.at/oebl_10/196.pdf|editor=Benda, K.|chapter=Schlesinger Ludwig (Lajos)|title=Österreichisches Biographisches Lexikon 1815–1950 (ÖBL)|volume=Band 10|publisher=Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften|location=Wien|year=1994|isbn=3-7001-2186-5|page=196}} Schlesinger's son Eilhard (1909–1968) immigrated in 1933 to Argentina and became there in 1944 a professor of Greek and classical Greek culture.</ref> His doctoral students include [[Abraham Plessner]].

Schlesinger was a [[historian of science]]. He wrote an article on the [[Complex analysis|function theory]] of [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] and translated [[René Descartes]]' ''[[La Géométrie]]'' into German (1894). He was one of the organizers of the celebrations for the hundredth anniversary of [[János Bolyai]] and from 1904 to 1909 with R. Fuchs he collected the works of his teacher Lazarus Fuchs, who was also his father-in-law. In 1902 he became a corresponding member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]]. In 1909 he received the [[Lobachevsky Prize]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Lapin, Sergey Alexandrovich|title=Nikolay Ivanovich Lobachevsky: Copernicus of Geometry (section on Lobachevsky Prize)|website=Mathematics Department, Washington State University (math.wsu.edu)|url=http://www.math.wsu.edu/faculty/slapin/research/presentations/Lobachevsky.pdf}} (slides for course MATH 398: Mathematical Snapshots. "Character, life work, and historical importance of mathematicians from various eras and branches of mathematics")</ref>

From 1929 until his death he was co-editor of ''[[Crelle's Journal]]''.

Like his teacher Fuchs, he worked primarily on linear [[ordinary differential equations]]. His two-volume ''Handbuch der Theorie der Linearen Differentialgleichungen'' was published from 1895 to 1898 in Teubner in Leipzig (Vol.2 in two parts).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Bôcher, Maxime|authorlink=Maxime Bôcher|title=Review: ''Handbuch der Theorie der Linearen Differentialgleichungen'', by Ludwig Schlesinger|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1897|volume=3|issue=4|pages=146–153|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1897-03-04/S0002-9904-1897-00387-1/|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1897-00387-1|doi-access=free}}</ref> He also published ''Einführung in die Theorie der gewöhnlichen Differentialgleichungen auf funktionentheoretischer Grundlage'' (Auflage, 1922), ''Vorlesungen über lineare Differentialgleichungen'' (1908)<ref>{{cite journal|author=Wilczynski, E. J.|authorlink=Ernest Julius Wilczynski|title=Review: ''Vorlesungen über lineare Differentialgleichungen'', by Ludwig Schlesinger|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1910|volume=16|issue=9|pages=483–489|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1910-16-09/S0002-9904-1910-01948-0/|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1910-01948-0|doi-access=free}}</ref> and ''Automorphe Funktionen'' (Gruyter, 1924). In 1909 he wrote a long report for the annual report of the German Mathematical Society on the history of linear differential equations since 1865.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Schlesinger, Ludwig|title=Bericht über die Entwicklung der Theorie der linearen Differentialgleichungen seit 1865|journal=Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung|volume=18|year=1909|pages=133–266|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/008899129}}</ref> He also studied differential geometry, and wrote a book of lectures on [[Albert Einstein]]'s [[general relativity theory]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Schlesinger, Ludwig|title=Raum, Zeit und Relativitätstheorie: gemeinverständliche Vorträge|series=Abhandlungen und Vorträge aus dem Gebiete der Mathematik, Naturwissenschaft und Technik; Heft 5 |publisher=Teubner|location=Leipzig|year=1920|url=https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/011678988}}</ref>

Today, his best known work is ''Über eine Klasse von Differentialsystemen beliebiger Ordnung mit festen kritischen Punkten'' (Crelle's Journal, 1912). There he considered the problem of [[isomonodromy deformation]]s for a certain matrix [[Regular singular point|Fuchsian equation]]; this is a special case of [[Hilbert's 21st Problem]] (existence of differential equations with prescribed monodromy). The paper introduced what are today called Schlesinger transformations and [[Schlesinger equations]].
